questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old elderly male presented with persistent fatigue and lymph total leucocyte count of 50,000/ul. His peripheral smear was done and had the findings as shown. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Flow cytometry

 

The image provided shows the presence of smudge cells, which are characteristic of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL). Smudge cells appear due to the fragility of leukemic cells, which easily break during slide preparation. The fragility is attributed to a defect in vimentin, a cytoskeletal protein. This results in the presence of crushed lymphocytes, a hallmark finding in CLL.

 

To confirm the diagnosis of CLL, the investigation of choice is flow cytometry. Flow cytometry is used to analyze cell surface markers, specifically looking for CD5 and CD23 positivity, which are characteristic markers of CLL. The presence of these markers differentiates CLL from other lymphoproliferative disorders, such as mantle cell lymphoma, which is CD5 positive but CD23 negative.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bone marrow aspirate: While a bone marrow aspirate can provide additional information, it is not the first-line test for diagnosing CLL. CLL primarily involves the peripheral blood and lymph nodes, with relatively less involvement of the bone marrow in early stages. Thus, bone marrow aspirate is not the preferred diagnostic test at this stage.

 

Option B. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH): FISH is useful for detecting chromosomal abnormalities and translocations in hematologic malignancies. It is particularly useful in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) to detect BCR-ABL translocation. However, in CLL, FISH is not the first diagnostic step but may be used later for prognostic evaluation (e.g., detecting deletion 17p for poor prognosis).

 

Option D. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): PCR is primarily used for detecting specific gene mutations or translocations in hematologic malignancies. For instance, it is useful for detecting BCR-ABL in CML. However, PCR is not the preferred initial test for CLL, as it does not provide the necessary immunophenotypic characterization.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: All of the following can be useful for differentiating megaloblastic anemia due to folate and B12 deficiency except?

options.label: B
options.text: Elevated serum levels of methyl malonyl CoA

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical history of specific dietary habits

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Elevated serum levels of homocysteine

 

Megaloblastic anemia is commonly caused by deficiencies of vitamin B12 or folate, leading to impaired DNA synthesis and characteristic hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear. Differentiating between B12 and folate deficiency is crucial because improper treatment (e.g., giving folic acid alone in B12 deficiency) can worsen neurological symptoms.

 

Why Homocysteine Levels Are Not a Useful Differentiator?

 

  • Both B12 and folate deficiencies lead to elevated homocysteine levels because both vitamins are required for homocysteine metabolism.
  • Since homocysteine is elevated in both conditions, it does not help differentiate between the two causes of megaloblastic anemia.
    • A strict vegan diet or "toast and tea" diet suggests B12 deficiency.
    • A diet lacking green leafy vegetables suggests folate deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Presence of neurological symptoms: Neurological symptoms (e.g., paresthesia, ataxia, cognitive decline) are specific to B12 deficiency and absent in folate deficiency, making it a key distinguishing factor.

 

Option B. Elevated serum levels of methyl malonyl CoA: This is only elevated in B12 deficiency, making it a distinguishing marker between the two conditions.

 

Option C. Clinical history of specific dietary habits: Dietary history is crucial in differentiation:

 

Educational Objective:

 

Both folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies lead to elevated homocysteine levels, because both are required for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine.

 

To differentiate between megaloblastic anemia due to folate or B12 deficiency, remember:

 

  • Neurological symptoms and elevated methyl malonyl CoA levels indicate B12 deficiency.
  • Folate deficiency does not cause neurological symptoms.
  • Homocysteine levels are elevated in both conditions and are not useful for differentiation.

questions.stem: In case of a FNAC thyroid, which of the following is a standard criteria for calling it as an adequate sample?

options.label: A
options.text: Atleast 10 groups of minimum 6 follicular cells each

options.label: B
options.text: Atleast 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: C
options.text: Atleast 3 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: D
options.text: Atleast 10 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

questions.answerText: Atleast 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atleast 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

 

Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) is widely used for evaluating thyroid nodules. However, the adequacy of the sample plays a crucial role in determining its diagnostic reliability.

 

According to the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology, an FNAC sample is considered adequate if it contains at least 6 groups of follicular cells, with each group containing at least 10 follicular cells. This criterion ensures a sufficient cellular sample for accurate cytological evaluation and classification.

 

Furthermore, FNAC is not useful in distinguishing between benign and malignant follicular neoplasms. Follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma can only be differentiated based on capsular or vascular invasion, which requires histopathological examination of an excised specimen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Bethesda System for Thyroid Cytopathology defines an adequate FNAC sample as having at least 6 groups of follicular cells, each containing at least 10 follicular cells. This criterion ensures sufficient cellularity for accurate cytological assessment and classification.

questions.stem: Which of the following takes place at the time of neutrophil extracellular trap formation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Arginine to citrulline

 

Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) are web-like structures composed of decondensed chromatin and antimicrobial proteins released by neutrophils in response to infections. This process, known as NETosis, helps trap and neutralize pathogens but is also implicated in autoimmune diseases.

 

The formation of NETs involves the enzyme arginine deiminase, which catalyzes the conversion of arginine to citrulline. This enzymatic reaction is a crucial part of NETosis, as citrullination of histones leads to chromatin decondensation, facilitating the extrusion of NETs.

 

One downside of NET formation is that it can contribute to the development of autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), where NET components can trigger an immune response against self-DNA.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Homocysteine to methionine: Incorrect. This reaction is part of the methionine cycle in biochemistry, facilitated by methionine synthase and vitamin B12. It plays no role in NET formation.

 

Option B. Methionine to homocysteine: Incorrect. This is part of amino acid metabolism, specifically the methionine-homocysteine cycle, and is unrelated to NETosis.

 

Option C. Glutamic acid to valine: Incorrect. This is associated with sickle cell disease (SCD), where a point mutation leads to the substitution of glutamic acid with valine in the β-globin chain, causing hemoglobin polymerization and sickle-shaped red blood cells. It is unrelated to neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) are formed through histone citrullination, which occurs via arginine to citrulline conversion by the enzyme arginine deiminase. NETosis plays a role in host defense but is also linked to autoimmune diseases like SLE.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presented with cola colored urine and had a history of skin infection few days back. His creatinine value was initially 2.5 mg/dl but even after 3 weeks of treatment it increased to 4.5 mg/dl. Which of the following is a likely kidney biopsy finding on electron microscopy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Subepithelial deposits

 

A child with skin infection followed by passage of cola colored urine is suggestive of post streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The worsening of creatinine from 2.5mg/dl to 4.5 mg/dl is suggestive of worsen of his condition in a short span of time. This prompts a diagnosis of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).

 

Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN):

 

  • Pathology: RPGN is characterized by the presence of crescents in the glomeruli, which are formed by the proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and infiltration of monocytes and macrophages.
  • Clinical Features: Rapid deterioration of renal function, often following an infection such as streptococcal throat or skin infection.
  • Crescents can be seen on light microscopy in RPGN (especially crescentic PSGN).
  • But electron microscopy (EM) will still show subepithelial deposits, which is diagnostic of PSGN.
  • So, even though the clinical course is RPGN, the question asked what you see on EM - hence the correct answer is Subepithelial deposits
    • Type I: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome)
    • Type II: Immune complex-mediated (e.g., PSGN, lupus nephritis)
    • Type III: Pauci-immune (e.g., Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis, also known as Wegener’s)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subendothelial deposits: Seen in conditions like lupus nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, not typical for RPGN following PSGN.

 

Option C. Crescents in glomeruli: Suggest RPGN, but the specific hallmark of PSGN is subepithelial humps (crescents may appear if it evolves into RPGN, but not diagnostic)

 

Option D. Mesangial deposits: Commonly seen in IgA nephropathy and other mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis, not specific for RPGN

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of crescents in the glomeruli on kidney biopsy is characteristic of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), especially in a patient with worsening renal function following an episode of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a correctly matched option?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Masson Fontana: collagen

 

The incorrect match is Masson Fontana and Collagen:

 

  • Masson Fontana stain is NOT for collagen; it is used to identify melanin and argentaffin granules (such as those in neuroendocrine cells).
  • The correct stain for collagen is Masson’s Trichrome, which stains collagen fibers blue or green, distinguishing them from muscle fibers and other structures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alizarin Red: Calcium (Correct): Used to stain calcium deposits in tissues.

 

Option C. Oil Red O: Lipid (Correct): A lipophilic dye used to stain neutral lipids in frozen sections. Also, Sudan Black is another lipid stain.

 

Option D. Feulgen: DNA (Correct): A DNA-specific stain that reacts with aldehydes from acid hydrolysis of DNA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Masson Fontana stains melanin, NOT collagen.
  • Masson’s Trichrome is the correct stain for collagen fibers.
  • Alizarin Red detects calcium, Oil Red O detects lipids, and Feulgen stain is specific for DNA.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with a history of chronic liver disease presents with abdominal pain, jaundice, and ascites. Laboratory tests reveal elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin levels. A liver biopsy is performed, which shows hepatocyte injury and apoptosis. Which of the following molecular events is most likely responsible for the initiation of the apoptosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Upregulation of pro-apoptotic Fas ligand

 

The patient’s history of chronic liver disease with ongoing hepatocyte apoptosis suggests extrinsic (death receptor-mediated) apoptosis, which is primarily mediated by the Fas-Fas ligand (FasL) pathway.

 

  1. Fas ligand (FasL) binds to Fas receptor (CD95), leading to apoptosis initiation.
  2. Fas-FasL interaction activates caspase-8, which then activates downstream executioner caspases such as caspase-3, leading to programmed cell death.
  3. This pathway is prominent in liver diseases, including viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and chronic liver damage.

 

Thus, upregulation of Fas ligand is the key molecular event responsible for initiating apoptosis in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Activation of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 proteins: Bcl-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that prevents apoptosis by stabilizing mitochondrial membranes and inhibiting cytochrome c release. If Bcl-2 were activated, apoptosis would be suppressed, not initiated.

 

Option B. Activation of caspase-3: Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase and is involved in the later stages of apoptosis. The question specifically asks about initiation of apoptosis, which occurs before caspase-3 activation.

 

Option D. Inhibition of p53: p53 promotes apoptosis in response to DNA damage. If p53 were inhibited, apoptosis would be reduced, which contradicts the presence of ongoing hepatocyte apoptosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Fas-Fas ligand interaction (CD95-CD95L) is a key initiator of apoptosis in hepatocyte injury.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and petechiae. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows myeloblasts comprising more than 20% of the total white blood cells. A bone marrow biopsy confirms the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Further molecular testing reveals the presence of a fusion gene involving the RUNX1-RUNX1T1 translocation. Which of the following statements best describes this genetic abnormality in AML?

options.label: A
options.text: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered an adverse prognostic factor.

options.label: B
options.text: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered a favorable prognostic factor.

options.label: C
options.text: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with AML-M5 subtype and is characterized by the presence of Auer rods.

options.label: D
options.text: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with AML-M3 subtype and is characterized by a t(15;17) translocation.

questions.answerText: RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered a favorable prognostic factor.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered a favorable prognostic factor.

 

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is classified based on genetic and cytogenetic abnormalities. The RUNX1-RUNX1T1 fusion gene results from the t(8;21) translocation, which is part of the core-binding factor (CBF) AML subtypes.

 

Key Points:

 

  • t(8;21) (RUNX1-RUNX1T1) is associated with AML-M2 (AML with maturation).
  • It falls under the category of Core Binding Factor AML, which generally carries a favorable prognosis.
  • Core Binding Factor AML includes:
    • t(8;21) RUNX1-RUNX1T1
    • inv(16) or t(16;16) (CBFB-MYH11)
  • Patients with core-binding factor AML respond well to chemotherapy and have better survival rates.

 

Thus, the correct answer is that RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered a favorable prognostic factor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with core-binding factor AML and is considered an adverse prognostic factor: 

 

  • Core-binding factor AML (including t(8;21) and inv(16)) is associated with a favorable prognosis, not an adverse one.
  • However, additional mutations (like KIT mutations) may worsen prognosis in some cases.

 

Option C. RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with AML-M5 subtype and is characterized by the presence of Auer rods:

 

  • AML-M5 (acute monocytic leukemia) is not associated with RUNX1-RUNX1T1.
  • AML-M5 is characterized by monocytic proliferation, gum hypertrophy, and CD14/CD11c positivity.
  • Auer rods can be seen in AML-M2 (t(8;21)) and AML-M3 (APL), but they are not exclusive to AML-M5.

 

Option D. RUNX1-RUNX1T1 is associated with AML-M3 subtype and is characterized by a t(15;17) translocation:

 

  • AML-M3 (Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia, APL) is characterized by t(15;17), PML-RARA fusion gene, and is treated with ATRA (All-Trans Retinoic Acid).
  • RUNX1-RUNX1T1 has NO role in AML-M3.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • AML with t(8;21) (RUNX1-RUNX1T1) is a core-binding factor AML with a favorable prognosis.
  • AML-M3 (APL) is characterized by t(15;17) (PML-RARA).
  • AML-M5 (acute monocytic leukemia) is not associated with RUNX1-RUNX1T1.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the red cell membrane protein responsible for most severe subtype of hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Spectrin

 

Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS) is a hemolytic anemia caused by defects in RBC membrane proteins, leading to loss of membrane integrity and early destruction of RBCs by the spleen.

 

  • Spectrin deficiency is associated with the most severe form of HS. Spectrin is a major structural cytoskeletal protein that maintains RBC shape and flexibility.
  • Severe spectrin deficiency results in membrane instability, extreme fragility, and increased hemolysis, leading to a more severe clinical phenotype requiring frequent transfusions or splenectomy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ankyrin: 

 

  • Most common cause of HS (~50-60% of cases).
  • Leads to mild-to-moderate disease, not the most severe form.

 

Option B. Band 4: 

 

  • Band 3 (AE1) mutation occurs in 15-30% of HS cases.
  • Causes moderate HS, not the most severe.

 

Option D. Glycophorin A: 

 

  • Not a structural protein involved in HS pathogenesis.
  • Primarily involved in MNS blood group system, not RBC membrane stability.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Ankyrin deficiency is the most common cause but results in a milder disease.
  • The most severe form of hereditary spherocytosis is caused by spectrin deficiency, leading to extreme RBC fragility and severe hemolysis. 

 

Key Features of Severe Hereditary Spherocytosis:

 

  • Genetic Basis: Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, often due to mutations in the SPTA1 gene
  • Protein Deficiency: Severe deficiency of alpha-spectrin
  • Clinical Manifestations: Severe anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and increased risk of gallstones
  • Treatment: Splenectomy is often necessary to manage severe cases

questions.stemHtml: Match the following complement deficiencies with the disorders given:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c 

 

Complement deficiencies impair the immune response, increasing susceptibility to specific infections and disorders.

 

  1. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency → Hereditary angioneurotic edema (b)
    • C1 inhibitor regulates the complement and kallikrein-kinin system.
    • Deficiency leads to uncontrolled bradykinin production, causing episodic swelling (angioedema) without urticaria.
  2. C3 deficiency → Pyogenic infections (d)
    • C3 is central to the complement cascade.
    • Deficiency results in impaired opsonization, leading to recurrent bacterial infections, particularly with encapsulated organisms (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae).
  3. Factor H deficiency → Hemolytic uremic syndrome (a)
    • Factor H regulates alternative complement pathway.
    • Deficiency leads to uncontrolled complement activation, which damages endothelial cells, causing hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) characterized by hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
  4. C5 to C8 deficiency → Recurrent Neisseria infections (c)
    • These late complement components are essential for membrane attack complex (MAC) formation, crucial for killing gram-negative bacteria like Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitidis.
    • Deficiency leads to increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema due to unregulated bradykinin production.
  • C3 deficiency leads to recurrent pyogenic infections due to defective opsonization.
  • Factor H deficiency is linked to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) due to uncontrolled complement activation.
  • C5-C8 deficiencies impair the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), increasing the risk of recurrent Neisseria infections.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about “liquid biopsy” in comparison to standard tissue biopsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor

options.label: C
options.text: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

questions.answerText: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

 

A liquid biopsy is a minimally invasive alternative to standard tissue biopsy, primarily used in oncology. It involves analyzing circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), exosomes, and other biomarkers from blood, urine, or other body fluids.

 

The amount of tumor-derived material in a liquid biopsy is significantly lower than that in a standard tissue biopsy. This makes detailed histopathological and molecular analysis more challenging.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Easier to perform: Liquid biopsy requires only a blood sample, unlike surgical or needle biopsies, making it easier and quicker to perform.

 

Option B. Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor: Liquid biopsy allows real-time monitoring of tumor evolution, detecting metastatic subclones that may differ from the primary tumor.

 

Option D. Less invasive: Unlike traditional biopsies, which require surgical or needle procedures, liquid biopsy is less invasive, reducing patient discomfort and complications.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Liquid biopsy is less invasive, easier to perform, and useful for detecting metastatic tumor subclones.
  • However, the amount of biological sample obtained is significantly lower compared to standard tissue biopsy, making it difficult for detailed molecular analysis.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presents with low grade fever, malaise and enlarged cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. The biopsy from one of the cervical nodes shows effaced architecture and sheet-like growth of small sized lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours (as in image). Immunohistochemical analysis shows positivity for pan B cell markers, CD5 and cyclin D1. The diagnosis in this case is.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mantle cell lymphoma

 

The provided histopathological image shows a monotonous proliferation of small lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours, which is highly suggestive of mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). The immunophenotypic markers confirm the diagnosis:

 

  1. CD5 positivity – MCL is a CD5-positive B-cell lymphoma.
  2. Cyclin D1 positivity – A hallmark of MCL, resulting from t(11;14) translocation, leading to overexpression of cyclin D1, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation.
  3. Effaced lymph node architecture – A typical feature of aggressive lymphomas, including MCL.

 

MCL typically presents in middle-aged or older men with generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and bone marrow involvement. It is more aggressive than other small B-cell lymphomas, with a poor prognosis despite initial responsiveness to chemotherapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Follicular lymphoma:

 

  • Follicular lymphoma lacks CD5 and cyclin D1 expression.
  • It typically shows follicular growth patterns, unlike the sheet-like growth in this case.

 

Option B. Hairy cell leukemia:

 

  • Hairy cell leukemia is a CD5-negative B-cell neoplasm.
  • It is characterized by TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) positivity and a fried egg appearance of cells on histology, which is absent here.

 

Option D. Marginal zone lymphoma:

 

  • Marginal zone lymphoma is associated with chronic inflammation (e.g., H. pylori infection in gastric MALT lymphoma).
  • It is CD5-negative and cyclin D1-negative, making it unlikely in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mantle cell lymphoma is characterized by CD5 and cyclin D1 positivity, due to t(11;14) translocation.
  • It is more aggressive than other small B-cell lymphomas, with a poor prognosis.
  • Differential diagnosis includes follicular lymphoma (CD5-negative), hairy cell leukemia (CD5-negative, TRAP-positive), and marginal zone lymphoma (CD5-negative, associated with chronic inflammation).

questions.stem: A patient presented with fever, weight loss and night sweats. He had 2 previous episodes of hemoptysis. His radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the right lung. Which of the following is the mechanism of cavitation in his lungs?

options.label: A
options.text: Mast cell degranulation due to cross linking of IgE

options.label: B
options.text: Vasculitis due to immune complex formation

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Delayed type hypersensitivity reaction

 

The patient's clinical presentation of fever, weight loss, night sweats, hemoptysis, and cavitary lung lesions is highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB).

 

In TB, lung cavitation occurs due to a Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity (DTH) reaction (Type IV hypersensitivity), mediated by CD4+ T cells and macrophages. The immune response leads to the formation of caseating granulomas, which undergo necrosis and subsequent cavitation.

 

Key Mechanisms in Tuberculosis Cavitation:

 

  1. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects macrophages, leading to activation of T-helper 1 (Th1) cells.
  2. Th1 cells release interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), activating macrophages to produce TNF-α, which plays a role in granuloma formation.
  3. Necrotic granulomas (caseous necrosis) can liquefy, forming cavitary lesions, which further facilitate the spread of tubercle bacilli.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mast cell degranulation due to cross-linking of IgE: Incorrect.

 

  • This describes a Type I hypersensitivity reaction, which occurs in allergic conditions (e.g., asthma, anaphylaxis) and is not related to tuberculosis or cavitation.

 

Option B. Vasculitis due to immune complex formation: Incorrect.

 

  • This describes a Type III hypersensitivity reaction, seen in conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
  • TB-related cavitation is not caused by immune complex deposition but by cell-mediated immunity.

 

Option D. Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity: Incorrect.

 

  • This describes a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, which involves complement activation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).
  • Seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, myasthenia gravis, and Graves’ disease, not in tuberculosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Lung cavitation in tuberculosis results from a Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity (DTH) reaction (Type IV hypersensitivity), mediated by CD4+ T cells and macrophages.
  • Caseous necrosis within granulomas leads to liquefaction and cavitation, promoting further bacterial spread.
  • TB-related cavitation is not caused by antibody-mediated, IgE-mediated, or immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity reactions.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman has noted painless enlargement of her neck for the past month. On physical examination she has diffuse, symmetrical thyroid enlargement without tenderness on palpation. Laboratory studies show her serum TSH is elevated but serum thyroxine is lower side of normal limits. Her microscopic examination is shown here. Which of the following laboratory test findings is she most likely to have?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) High anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titre

 

The patient's diffuse, painless thyroid enlargement, elevated TSH with low-normal thyroxine, and histopathological findings of lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers are characteristic of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder where autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) attack the thyroid gland, leading to progressive hypothyroidism.
  • The hallmark laboratory finding in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is high titers of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies, which are present in >90% of cases.

 

Over time, the destruction of thyroid follicles results in fibrosis and atrophy, leading to permanent hypothyroidism, requiring lifelong levothyroxine replacement therapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased serum calcitonin: Elevated calcitonin is seen in medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which is associated with C-cell hyperplasia and RET proto-oncogene mutations, not Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

Option C. Increased serum parathormone: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases in primary hyperparathyroidism, which is unrelated to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

 

Option D. Positive antinuclear antibody test: While autoimmune thyroid disorders can be associated with ANA positivity, it is not a specific diagnostic marker for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. ANA is more commonly used for diagnosing systemic autoimmune diseases like lupus (SLE).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by high anti-TPO antibody titers and lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation.
  • It leads to hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low-normal/free T4 levels.
  • Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice.

questions.stem: A young female Basanti presents with recurrent thromboses, repeated miscarriages, cardiac valve vegetations, and thrombocytopenia. Laboratory tests reveal the presence of lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies in the blood. Which of the following is the most plausible explanation for her recurrent fetal loss?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibody mediated thrombocytopenia leading to excessive bleeding

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody mediated thrombosis of placental vessels

options.label: C
options.text: Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts

questions.answerText: Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts

 

The patient’s history of recurrent thrombosis, pregnancy loss, cardiac valve vegetations, and presence of lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies is highly suggestive of Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APLS).

 

  • APLS is an autoimmune disorder associated with hypercoagulability and recurrent pregnancy loss.
  • The current pathophysiological concept states that autoantibodies (especially anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 antibodies) interfere with trophoblast differentiation, leading to failed implantation and early pregnancy loss.
  • This is the primary mechanism behind recurrent fetal loss in APLS, rather than placental thrombosis, which was previously believed to be the main cause.

 

Additionally, APLS is characterized by prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), despite a hypercoagulable state, due to lupus anticoagulant effects.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Antibody-mediated thrombocytopenia leading to excessive bleeding: Incorrect.

 

  • Thrombocytopenia can occur in APLS, but it does not lead to fetal loss due to excessive bleeding.
  • The primary cause of pregnancy loss in APLS is trophoblast dysfunction, not hemorrhagic complications.

 

Option B. Antibody-mediated thrombosis of placental vessels: Incorrect.

 

  • Although APLS is a prothrombotic disorder, recent research suggests that fetal loss occurs due to trophoblast dysfunction rather than placental thrombosis.
  • While placental thrombosis may contribute, it is not the primary mechanism of fetal loss in APLS.

 

Option D. Antibody-mediated cardiac dysfunction: Incorrect.

 

  • APLS can lead to cardiac complications, such as Libman-Sacks endocarditis (nonbacterial thrombotic vegetations).
  • However, cardiac dysfunction does not directly cause recurrent pregnancy loss in APLS.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Recurrent pregnancy loss in Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome (APLS) is primarily due to antibody-mediated interference with trophoblast differentiation, not thrombosis.
  • APLS is associated with autoantibodies like anti-β2 glycoprotein 1, lupus anticoagulant, and anticardiolipin antibodies.
  • A prolonged aPTT is seen in APLS despite a hypercoagulable state.

questions.stem: You are working in a hospital where you are training blood bank technicians about blood components. Which of the following blood component does not show ABO incompatibility?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cryoprecipitate 

 

When transfusing blood components, ABO compatibility is crucial for most products, particularly those containing plasma and red blood cell antigens. However, cryoprecipitate does not show ABO incompatibility and can be transfused without strict ABO matching.

 

Key Concepts:

 

  • Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) contain plasma proteins and antibodies, requiring ABO compatibility to prevent hemolysis or immune reactions.
  • Single donor platelets also express minor ABO antigens, and ABO matching is preferred for optimal transfusion efficacy.
  • Cryoprecipitate is primarily composed of clotting factors (Factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, Factor XIII, and fibronectin) and contains minimal plasma, making ABO incompatibility insignificant.

 

Even though it is ideal to transfuse ABO-matched cryoprecipitate, it does not cause major reactions if mismatched.

 

Clinical Uses of Cryoprecipitate:

 

  • Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)
  • Von Willebrand disease (vWF deficiency)
  • Hypofibrinogenemia (low fibrinogen levels in bleeding patients)

 

For other coagulation factor deficiencies (e.g., Hemophilia B or Factor IX deficiency), fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is used instead of cryoprecipitate.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fresh frozen plasma: Contains plasma proteins and antibodies, requiring ABO compatibility to prevent hemolysis.

 

Option B. Platelet-rich plasma: Platelets express ABO antigens, and plasma contains antibodies, necessitating ABO matching for better efficacy.

 

Option C. Single donor platelets: ABO matching is preferred, as platelets contain some ABO antigens, and transfusion from a mismatched donor can reduce platelet survival and function.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cryoprecipitate does not show significant ABO incompatibility and can be transfused regardless of blood group.
  • Fresh frozen plasma, platelet-rich plasma, and single donor platelets require ABO compatibility due to the presence of antigens and antibodies.
  • Cryoprecipitate is used primarily for Hemophilia A, von Willebrand disease, and hypofibrinogenemia.

questions.stem: Pick the incorrect statement about major histocompatibility complex?

options.label: A
options.text: MHC I molecule has 1 long chain, 1 short chain

options.label: B
options.text: MHC II molecule has 2 equal length chains

options.label: C
options.text: No two individuals are ever likely to express the same MHC molecules

options.label: D
options.text: Difference in MHC haplotype causes increased risk of organ rejection between 2 people

questions.answerText: No two individuals are ever likely to express the same MHC molecules
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) No two individuals are ever likely to express the same MHC molecules

 

The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) plays a crucial role in the immune response, helping to present antigens to T cells. It consists of two classes:

 

  • MHC I (expressed on all nucleated cells) – Presents antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
  • MHC II (expressed on antigen-presenting cells like macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells) – Presents antigens to CD4+ helper T cells.

 

While MHC molecules are highly polymorphic, making it unlikely for unrelated individuals to have identical MHC molecules, identical twins can have the same MHC molecules because they inherit the exact same genetic material. Therefore, the statement that "No two individuals are ever likely to express the same MHC molecules" is incorrect because identical twins are an exception.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. MHC I molecule has 1 long chain, 1 short chain: Correct. MHC I is composed of one long α-chain (α1, α2, α3) and one short β2-microglobulin chain.

 

Option B. MHC II molecule has 2 equal-length chains: Correct. MHC II is composed of two chains of equal length: α (α1, α2) and β (β1, β2).

 

Option D. Difference in MHC haplotype causes increased risk of organ rejection between two people: Correct. MHC (HLA) mismatches increase the risk of organ rejection due to T-cell-mediated immune responses against non-self MHC molecules.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Identical twins, however, can have the same MHC molecules, making the statement "No two individuals are ever likely to express the same MHC molecules" incorrect.
  • No two individuals (other than identical twins) are likely to express the same MHC molecules
  • MHC I present endogenous antigens (eg, viral or cytosolic proteins) to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells 
  • MHC II present exogenous antigens (eg, bacterial proteins) to CD4+ helper T cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an autoimmune disorder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ulcerative colitis

 

An autoimmune disorder is characterized by an immune system attack against specific self-antigens, leading to tissue damage. To classify a disease as autoimmune, a well-defined autoantigen or autoantibody must be identified.

 

  • Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory disorder, but no specific autoantigen has been identified.
  • It is part of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), which results from immune dysregulation rather than a direct autoimmune attack.
  • While immune system abnormalities contribute to chronic inflammation in the colon, the absence of a well-defined autoantigen excludes it from classical autoimmune diseases.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Grave’s disease:

 

  • Autoimmune attack on the TSH receptor leads to thyroid hormone overproduction (hyperthyroidism).
  • TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) are characteristic.

 

Option C. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): 

 

  • Autoimmune attack against synovial joints leads to chronic joint inflammation.
  • Rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are present.

 

Option D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): 

 

  • Multi-system autoimmune disease affecting skin, kidneys, joints, and blood cells.
  • Characterized by antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-dsDNA, and anti-Smith antibodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Ulcerative colitis is an immune-mediated disorder but lacks a well-defined autoantigen, so it is not classified as an autoimmune disease.
  • True autoimmune diseases (e.g., Grave’s disease, RA, SLE) involve a specific autoantigen and autoantibodies.
  • Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, both driven by immune dysregulation rather than direct autoimmune mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about activated partial thromboplastin time to:

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate refrigeration to preserve factor viability

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Activated with kaolin 

 

Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) is a laboratory test used to assess the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, particularly factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. It is commonly used to monitor heparin therapy and diagnose coagulation disorders.

 

  • aPTT requires an activating agent to initiate clotting.
  • Kaolin (or silica) is used as the activating agent, providing a negatively charged surface to facilitate clotting factor activation.

 

The ideal conditions for performing aPTT include:

 

  • Using platelet-free plasma (not platelet-rich plasma).
  • Keeping the sample at room temperature (22-26°C) instead of refrigeration.
  • Performing the test within 2 hours of sample collection for accurate results.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Immediate refrigeration to preserve factor viability: Incorrect. Refrigeration can degrade labile clotting factors (Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor) and alter test results, so aPTT should be performed at room temperature (22-26°C).

 

Option B. Platelet-rich plasma is essential: Incorrect. Platelet-free plasma is used for aPTT because platelets do not contribute to plasma clotting factor analysis.

 

Option C. Done within 4 hours: Incorrect. The aPTT test should ideally be performed within 2 hours of sample collection for accurate measurement of clotting factor activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • aPTT is used to assess the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways and monitor heparin therapy.
  • Kaolin or silica is used as the activator in aPTT.
  • Refrigeration is avoided because it degrades clotting factors, and platelet-free plasma is required.
  • The test should be performed within 2 hours of sample collection at room temperature.

questions.stemHtml: You are working in a PHC and have to send a sample for blood glucose estimation. Which of the following vacutainers will you use for sending your sample?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) It contains potassium oxalate + sodium fluoride

 

For blood glucose estimation, it is essential to prevent glycolysis (the breakdown of glucose by red blood cells), which lowers glucose levels falsely if the sample is not processed immediately.

 

  • The gray-top vacutainer (D) contains sodium fluoride (NaF) and potassium oxalate:
    • Sodium fluoride inhibits enolase, an enzyme in glycolysis, preventing glucose degradation.
    • Potassium oxalate acts as an anticoagulant to prevent clot formation.

 

This ensures an accurate blood glucose measurement, even if the sample processing is delayed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blue-top vacutainer (Citrate tube): Incorrect. Contains sodium citrate, used for coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, D-dimer), not for glucose estimation.

 

Option B. Red-top vacutainer (Plain tube): Incorrect. Contains no anticoagulant or glycolysis inhibitor. It allows blood to clot, leading to serum separation, but does not prevent glucose breakdown.

 

Option C. Purple-top vacutainer (EDTA tube): Incorrect. Contains EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid), which is used for CBC, blood smears, and hematology studies. It does not prevent glycolysis, making it unsuitable for glucose estimation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • For blood glucose estimation, always use a gray-top vacutainer containing sodium fluoride (glycolysis inhibitor) and potassium oxalate (anticoagulant).
  • Other vacutainers (blue, red, purple) are used for coagulation studies, biochemistry, or hematology, but do not prevent glucose degradation.

questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old presented with intussusceptions and was found to be having a polyp. A biopsy is taken and is shown alongside. What is the likely diagnosis in this individual?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Peutz Jegher polyp 

 

The patient’s age (16 years), presence of intussusception, and histopathological findings of a polyp with an arborizing pattern suggest Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS).

 

Key Features of Peutz-Jeghers Polyp:

 

  • Hamartomatous polyp with arborizing (branching) smooth muscle fibers extending into the lamina propria.
  • Commonly found in the small intestine (jejunum, ileum), colon, and stomach.
  • Patients often present with intussusception due to the polyp acting as a lead point.
  • Associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by STK11 gene mutation.
  • Mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark spots on lips, oral mucosa, and hands) is a hallmark of this syndrome.

 

PJS is associated with an increased risk of gastrointestinal and extraintestinal malignancies, including colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, breast, and ovarian cancers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Juvenile polyp:

 

  • Juvenile polyps are hamartomatous but lack the arborizing smooth muscle seen in Peutz-Jeghers polyps.
  • They are mucin-filled and often found in the rectum.
  • Common in children, presenting with painless rectal bleeding.

 

Option B. Adenomatous polyp:

 

  • Adenomatous polyps (tubular, villous, or tubulovillous) are pre-malignant lesions associated with APC gene mutations.
  • They lack the arborizing smooth muscle pattern seen in Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

 

Option C. Tubulovillous polyp:

 

  • A mixed adenomatous polyp containing both tubular and villous components.
  • Higher malignant potential, but does not show the smooth muscle arborization characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Peutz-Jeghers polyp is a hamartomatous polyp with an arborizing smooth muscle pattern and is associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11 mutation).
  • Common presentation includes intussusception, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and increased cancer risk.
  • Arborising pattern on histology is associated with Peutz Jegher polyp.

questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old previously healthy man has noticed blood in his urine for the past 2 days Laboratory findings show a serum urea nitrogen level of 39 mg/dL and creatinine level of 4.1 mg/dL. A renal biopsy specimen is obtained; the immunofluorescence pattern of staining with antibody against human IgG is shown in the figure. Which of the following serologic findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody

 

The immunofluorescence image demonstrates a linear pattern of IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). This finding is characteristic of Goodpasture Syndrome, which is caused by anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies targeting type IV collagen (α3 chain) in the kidney and lungs.

 

Key Features of Goodpasture Syndrome:

 

  • Linear IgG deposits on immunofluorescence.
  • Glomerulonephritis with rapidly progressive renal failure.
  • Pulmonary hemorrhage leading to hemoptysis (Goodpasture Syndrome).
  • Serum anti-GBM antibodies targeting type IV collagen (α3 chain).

 

Goodpasture syndrome is classified under Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN Type 1) and can lead to crescent formation on light microscopy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Anti–streptolysin O antibody: 

 

  • Seen in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which shows a granular “lumpy-bumpy” pattern on immunofluorescence due to immune complex deposition.
  • Not associated with linear IgG deposits.

 

Option C. C3 nephritic factor: 

 

  • Found in Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN Type II or Dense Deposit Disease) due to alternative complement pathway activation.
  • Immunofluorescence in MPGN II shows C3 deposition in an "ribbon-like" pattern, not linear IgG deposits.

 

Option D. Hepatitis B surface antibody:

 

  • Associated with membranous nephropathy, which shows granular IgG and C3 deposits in a "spike and dome" pattern on silver stain.
  • Not linked to Goodpasture Syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Goodpasture Syndrome is an autoimmune disorder caused by anti-GBM antibodies targeting type IV collagen (α3 chain), leading to glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.
  • The hallmark of Goodpasture Syndrome is a linear IgG deposition pattern on immunofluorescence microscopy.
  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) shows a granular immune complex deposition, while MPGN and membranous nephropathy have distinct patterns on immunofluorescence.

questions.stem: A patient with intestinal malabsorption is found to markedly improve when flour products (bread, noodles, etc.) are removed from his diet. At the height of the patient’s disease, marked histologic changes would be seen at which of the following sites?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Proximal small bowel 

 

The patient’s symptoms suggest celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy), an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten ingestion. The disease primarily affects the proximal small intestine (duodenum and proximal jejunum), where gluten proteins trigger an immune-mediated inflammatory response, leading to villous atrophy and malabsorption.

 

Key Histologic Features in Celiac Disease:

 

  • Villous atrophy (flattened villi)
  • Crypt hyperplasia
  • Intraepithelial lymphocytosis
  • Loss of brush border enzymes (leading to lactose intolerance in some cases)

 

Since the duodenum is the primary site for iron absorption, patients with celiac disease often develop iron deficiency anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Distal large bowel: 

 

  • Celiac disease does not primarily affect the large bowel. The colon is relatively spared, except in rare cases of secondary inflammation due to severe malabsorption.

 

Option B. Distal small bowel:

 

  • The ileum (distal small bowel) is less affected, though in severe cases, inflammation may extend beyond the duodenum and proximal jejunum.
  • B12 absorption occurs in the ileum, but B12 deficiency is not a hallmark of celiac disease.

 

Option D. Entire small bowel:

 

  • While severe, long-standing cases may involve more extensive portions of the small intestine, the primary histologic changes are seen in the proximal small intestine (duodenum).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Celiac disease primarily affects the proximal small intestine (duodenum and proximal jejunum), leading to villous atrophy and malabsorption.
  • Common symptoms include diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, and iron deficiency anemia.
  • Histopathology reveals villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
  • A gluten-free diet leads to symptom resolution and mucosal healing.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has severe lower abdominal pain that radiates to the groin. He then notes blood in his urine. Which of the following substances is most likely to be increased in his urine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Calcium oxalate

 

The patient’s sudden onset of severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin, along with hematuria (blood in urine), suggests nephrolithiasis (kidney stone disease).

 

Most Common Type of Kidney Stones:

 

  • Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type (80% of kidney stones).
  • They form in acidic urine and appear as envelope-shaped (dihydrate) or dumbbell-shaped (monohydrate) crystals on urine microscopy.
  • Hypercalciuria (increased calcium in urine) and hyperoxaluria (increased oxalate in urine) are major risk factors.

 

Causes of Calcium Oxalate Stones:

 

  • Idiopathic hypercalciuria
  • Diet high in oxalate-rich foods (spinach, nuts, chocolate)
  • Low fluid intake (dehydration)
  • Hyperparathyroidism (increased calcium excretion)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mucoprotein: 

 

  • Mucoprotein forms the organic matrix of kidney stones, serving as a nidus (core) for crystal deposition.
  • However, it does not directly contribute to stone formation or appear in large amounts in urine.

 

Option B. Uric acid: 

 

  • Uric acid stones form in acidic urine and are associated with gout, chronic diarrhea, or high-purine diets.
  • Microscopically appear as rhomboid or rosette-shaped crystals.

 

Option C. Magnesium ammonium phosphate (Struvite stones): 

 

  • Struvite stones are associated with urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by urease-producing bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella, Ureaplasma urealyticum).
  • Microscopically appear as "coffin-lid" crystals.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stones and appear as envelope- or dumbbell-shaped crystals in urine.
  • Risk factors include hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and low fluid intake.
  • Other types of stones include uric acid (rhomboid), struvite (coffin-lid), and cystine (hexagonal) stones.

questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old college basketball player suddenly collapses on the court. A cardiac monitor shows ventricular tachycardia and then ventricular fibrillation. He is successfully resuscitated and hospitalized. The patient’s history indicates that his father died suddenly at 38 years of age. The boy’s echocardiogram reveals a thickened left ventricular wall, with a small slit-like chamber. The inter-ventricular septum is also markedly thickened. Five years later the patient expires suddenly. Histologic examination of the heart muscle at autopsy is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 

 

This case describes sudden cardiac arrest in a young athlete, a hallmark of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM). The family history of sudden death, left ventricular hypertrophy with asymmetric septal thickening, and myocyte disarray on histology confirm the diagnosis.

 

Key Features of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM):

 

  • Autosomal dominant disorder due to mutations in β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) or myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3).
  • Septal hypertrophy leads to left ventricular outflow obstruction.
  • Microscopic finding: Myocyte disarray ("helter-skelter arrangement") with interstitial fibrosis.
  • Presents with:
    • Exertional syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD) in young athletes.
    • Harsh systolic murmur, increased with Valsalva (due to worsened outflow obstruction).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Amyloidosis: Incorrect.

 

  • Amyloid deposits cause restrictive cardiomyopathy, leading to diastolic dysfunction, thickened myocardium, and apple-green birefringence on Congo red stain.
  • No myocyte disarray is seen.

 

Option B. Cardiac myxoma: Incorrect.

 

  • Most common primary cardiac tumor, typically arising in the left atrium.
  • Presents with syncope and embolic events, not ventricular arrhythmias or hypertrophy.

 

Option C. Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM): Incorrect.

 

  • Characterized by ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction.
  • Associated with alcohol, viral myocarditis, and genetic causes, but does not show myocyte disarray on histology.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in sarcomeric proteins, most commonly β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7).
  • Histologically, HCM is characterized by myocyte disarray and interstitial fibrosis.
  • It is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes due to ventricular arrhythmias.

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokines is primarily responsible for the formation of non-caseating granulomas in sarcoidosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha)

 

D Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) is preferred over C. Interleukin-12 (IL-12

 

Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by non-caseating granulomas composed of activated macrophages (epithelioid histiocytes) and multinucleated giant cells. The cytokine tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) plays a crucial role in granuloma formation and maintenance.

 

Pathogenesis of Granuloma Formation in Sarcoidosis:

 

  1. Antigenic trigger activates alveolar macrophages.
  2. Dendritic cells release IL-12, which stimulates Th1 differentiation.
  3. Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, activating macrophages.
  4. TNF-alpha promotes aggregation and maintenance of granulomas.

 

Clinical Significance of TNF-alpha in Sarcoidosis:

 

  • Increased TNF-alpha levels correlate with disease severity.
  • TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., infliximab) are used for refractory sarcoidosis.
  • Before initiating anti-TNF therapy, latent tuberculosis (TB) must be ruled out, as TNF-alpha is critical for controlling TB infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Interleukin-1 (IL-1)

 

  • IL-1 plays a role in inflammation and fever but is not the key driver of granuloma formation.

 

Option B. Interleukin-6 (IL-6)

 

  • IL-6 is involved in acute phase reactions and systemic inflammation, but it does not drive granuloma formation.

 

Option C. Interleukin-12 (IL-12) 

 

  • IL-12 activates Th1 cells, leading to IFN-gamma release, which promotes macrophage activation.
  • However, TNF-alpha is the primary cytokine responsible for granuloma maintenance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • TNF-alpha is the primary cytokine responsible for granuloma formation in sarcoidosis.
  • Th1 response (IL-12 → IFN-gamma → TNF-alpha) is critical for granuloma development.
  • TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g., infliximab) are used in refractory sarcoidosis but require tuberculosis screening before administration.
