questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with excessive bleeding following a minor injury. She has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. Laboratory testing reveals a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) that does not correct after mixing her plasma with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acquired factor VIII inhibitor

 

This patient presents with excessive bleeding and an isolated prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct with a mixing study, strongly suggesting the presence of an acquired factor VIII inhibitor (autoantibody against factor VIII).

 

Key Findings in Acquired Hemophilia:

 

  • Autoantibody against factor VIII disrupts the coagulation cascade.
  • Prolonged aPTT due to defective intrinsic pathway.
  • Mixing study does NOT correct aPTT because the inhibitor is still active.

 

Confirmatory Test:

 

  • Bethesda assay detects the presence of factor VIII inhibitors.

 

Causes of Acquired Factor VIII Inhibitor:

 

  • Idiopathic (most common)
  • Autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus)
  • Malignancies
  • Pregnancy/postpartum period
  • Certain drugs (penicillin, interferon, fludarabine, etc.)

 

Management:

 

  • First-line treatment: Immunosuppressive therapy (steroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide) to eliminate the autoantibody.
  • Acute bleeding episodes: Bypass agents such as recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) or activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilia A:

 

  • X-linked recessive disorder, typically seen in males.
  • Prolonged aPTT that corrects with a mixing study (no inhibitors).
  • Factor VIII deficiency is congenital, not acquired.

 

Option B. Von Willebrand disease (VWD):

 

  • VWD primarily causes mucosal bleeding (e.g., nosebleeds, menorrhagia), not prolonged aPTT without correction.
  • Mixing study corrects aPTT in VWD.

 

Option C. Factor IX deficiency (Hemophilia B):

 

  • X-linked disorder, typically affects males.
  • Prolonged aPTT corrects with mixing study (no inhibitor present).
  • Similar presentation to hemophilia A but involves factor IX deficiency instead of factor VIII.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Acquired factor VIII inhibitor is characterized by spontaneous development of autoantibodies against factor VIII, leading to excessive bleeding.
  • It presents with a prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct with a mixing study.
  • Confirmed by the Bethesda assay, it is treated with immunosuppression (steroids, rituximab) and bypass agents for bleeding control.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is correctly matched about liver tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b

 

  1. Hepatoblastoma → (d) Malignant tumor in children with high AFP levels
    • Hepatoblastoma is the most common malignant liver tumor in children.
    • It is associated with high levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).
    • Not a benign tumor (common misconception).
  2. Cavernous hemangioma → (c) Commonest benign tumor in which biopsy is contraindicated
    • Most common benign liver tumor.
    • Biopsy is contraindicated due to high risk of hemorrhage.
  3. Angiosarcoma → (a) Plastic pipe factory worker with vWF as marker
    • Highly aggressive malignant tumor of the liver.
    • Associated with exposure to vinyl chloride (plastic industry), arsenic, and thorotrast.
    • vWF (von Willebrand factor) is a marker.
  4. Fibrolamellar HCC → (b) Young adult with PRKACA-DNAJB1 oncogene (+)
    • Rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
    • Occurs in young adults without hepatitis B or cirrhosis.
    • Associated with PRKACA-DNAJB1 fusion oncogene.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hepatoblastoma is a malignant liver tumor in children with high AFP levels.
  • Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, and biopsy is contraindicated.
  • Angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride exposure and expresses vWF.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC occurs in young adults and is associated with PRKACA-DNAJB1 oncogene.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old tall male with long limbs presents with multiple painless mucosal nodules on the lips and tongue, thickening of the corneal nerves, and a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in his father. Physical examination reveals a ganglioneuroma on the posterior tongue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B)

 

  • This patient has a classic presentation of MEN2B, which is characterized by:
    • Marfanoid habitus (tall stature, long limbs)
    • Mucosal neuromas on the lips and tongue
    • Thickened corneal nerves
    • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which has a strong genetic component (family history present)
    • Pheochromocytoma, though not explicitly mentioned in this case
  • MEN2B is caused by a RET proto-oncogene mutation and is more aggressive than MEN2A.
  • Prophylactic thyroidectomy is advised in these patients due to the high risk of developing MTC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1):

 

  • MEN1 involves the "3 P’s": Pituitary adenomas, Parathyroid hyperplasia, and Pancreatic tumors.
  • No marfanoid habitus or mucosal neuromas are seen in MEN1.

 

Option B. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A):

 

  • MEN2A includes MTC, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia.
  • It lacks mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, making MEN2B the more accurate diagnosis.

 

Option D. Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (FMTC):

 

  • FMTC is a variant of MEN2 but only involves medullary thyroid carcinoma.
  • It does not have pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, or marfanoid habitus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • MEN2B is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, marfanoid habitus, and mucosal neuromas.
  • It is caused by a RET proto-oncogene mutation, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is strongly recommended.

questions.stem: An elderly patient dies due to a cancer and his cells in the cancer affected area were examined. Ultra structurally, the most prominent features found are the loss of mitochondrial cristae and ruptured outer mitochondrial membrane. Which of the following best can be the pattern of cell death here?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ferroptosis

 

  • Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death characterized by free radical-induced mitochondrial damage.
  • The loss of mitochondrial cristae and ruptured outer mitochondrial membrane seen ultrastructurally are hallmark features of ferroptosis.
  • Key features of ferroptosis include:
    • Iron accumulation leading to oxidative stress
    • Lipid peroxidation causing cell membrane damage
    • Glutathione peroxidase (GPX4) deficiency, which fails to neutralize oxidative stress
  • This mechanism is particularly implicated in cancer cell death, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and neurodegenerative disorders.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Necrosis:

 

  • Necrosis is unregulated cell death often due to ischemia or trauma.
  • Unlike ferroptosis, necrosis shows random cellular swelling and membrane rupture, without mitochondrial-specific damage.

 

Option B. Necroptosis:

 

  • Programmed necrosis, distinct from ferroptosis.
  • Mediated by RIPK1 and RIPK3 signaling, not iron accumulation.
  • No specific mitochondrial damage as seen in ferroptosis.

 

Option D. Pyroptosis:

 

  • Caspase-1 and caspase-11 dependent cell death, often triggered by infections.
  • Involves inflammasome activation and release of IL-1β and IL-18.
  • Membrane rupture occurs, but mitochondrial loss of cristae is not a feature.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death characterized by mitochondrial cristae loss and lipid peroxidation.
  • It is distinct from apoptosis, necrosis, and necroptosis.
  • Key regulators include iron metabolism and glutathione peroxidase (GPX4).

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with headaches, unsteady gait, and vomiting. Neurological examination reveals truncal ataxia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows a midline mass in the posterior fossa compressing the fourth ventricle. Histological analysis of the tumor demonstrates small, blue, undifferentiated cells with a high mitotic index. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Medulloblastoma 

 

  • Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children and arises from the cerebellum.
  • This tumor is classically found in the midline of the posterior fossa, leading to compression of the fourth ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
  • Truncal ataxia occurs due to cerebellar involvement.
  • Histological hallmarks include:
    • Small, blue, undifferentiated cells
    • High mitotic index
    • Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ependymoma:

 

  • Usually arises from the lining of the ventricles, most commonly fourth ventricle.
  • Causes hydrocephalus, but histologically shows perivascular pseudorosettes, not small blue cells.

 

Option C. Meningioma:

 

  • More common in adults, often associated with progesterone receptors.
  • Arises from meningothelial cells of the arachnoid, not a posterior fossa tumor in children.

 

Option D. Craniopharyngioma:

 

  • Derived from remnants of Rathke’s pouch and occurs suprasellar rather than posterior fossa.
  • Characterized by calcifications and a "machine oil" appearance in imaging, along with bitemporal hemianopia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, arising in the midline cerebellum and often causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
  • Histology shows small blue cells with high mitotic activity and Homer-Wright rosettes.
  • It commonly spreads via the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and may cause drop metastases in the spinal cord.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with a painful, swollen neck and fever. Physical examination reveals a tender and enlarged thyroid gland. Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and thyrotoxicosis with an increased serum concentration of free thyroxine (T4). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis

 

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis) is the most likely diagnosis in this case, as the condition is characterized by:

 

  1. Painful, swollen thyroid gland: A key feature differentiating this condition from other thyroid disorders.
  2. Fever and systemic symptoms: Common in the acute phase.
  3. Elevated ESR: Indicates inflammation, a hallmark of subacute thyroiditis.
  4. Transient thyrotoxicosis: Caused by the release of stored thyroid hormones due to inflammation and destruction of thyroid tissue.

 

This condition is often preceded by a viral infection and resolves spontaneously with symptomatic treatment, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Graves' disease: This is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism but typically presents with a painless goiter and other specific features, such as exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema. It is not associated with a tender thyroid.

 

Option B. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: This is a common cause of hypothyroidism and involves a painless enlargement of the thyroid. It is associated with lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of Hurthle cells, but not with acute pain or elevated ESR.

 

Option D. Toxic multinodular goiter: This condition causes hyperthyroidism due to autonomously functioning thyroid nodules but is not associated with thyroid pain, fever, or elevated ESR.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis): Painful, tender thyroid enlargement with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever) and transient thyrotoxicosis, typically following a viral illness.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney? It is the most common subtype of malignant renal tumorAssociated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3Arises from distal convoluted tubuleCells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1, 4  

 

1. Clear cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for 70-80% of cases.

 

4. Cells contain glycogen and lipid, which are dissolved during tissue processing, giving them a clear cytoplasm on histology.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Associated with loss of the long arm of chromosome 3: Incorrect. Clear cell carcinoma is associated with loss of the short arm (3p), not the long arm. The VHL gene is located on chromosome 3p and plays a role in tumor suppression.

 

3. Arises from the distal convoluted tubule: Incorrect. Clear cell carcinoma originates from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal convoluted tubule.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Clear cell carcinoma is the most common renal malignancy.
  • It arises from the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • It is associated with loss of chromosome 3p (VHL gene mutation).
  • Histologically, cells have clear cytoplasm due to glycogen and lipid accumulation.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following cell within cell phenomenon is associated with cellular process in which one cell enters into another cell without being degraded or destroyed?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Emperipolesis

 

  • Emperipolesis is a phenomenon where one cell enters another cell without being degraded or destroyed.
  • This process differs from phagocytosis, where the engulfed cell is digested.
  • It is commonly seen in conditions like Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy) and some leukemias and lymphomas.
  • Histologically, it appears as intact lymphocytes, neutrophils, or plasma cells within the cytoplasm of larger cells (histiocytes or megakaryocytes).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Entosis 

 

  • In entosis, one live cell enters another and is later degraded.
  • This occurs in some cancers and is associated with cell competition.

 

Option B. Efferocytosis 

 

  • This process involves the clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages to prevent inflammation.
  • It is a part of normal immune system function.

 

Option D. Encleisis 

 

  • A rare term, encleisis describes partial engulfment without digestion, but it is not commonly used in pathology.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Emperipolesis is a process in which one cell enters another without being degraded.
  • It is seen in Rosai-Dorfman disease, leukemias, and some hematologic disorders.
  • It differs from entosis (which leads to degradation) and efferocytosis (which clears apoptotic cells).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct statement about liquid biopsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid biopsy primarily relies on the analysis of tissue samples obtained through surgical procedures.

options.label: B
options.text: It is mainly used for the diagnosis of infectious diseases and not for cancer detection.

options.label: C
options.text: Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.

options.label: D
options.text: Liquid biopsy is only used to determine the exact stage of cancer but not for initial detection.

questions.answerText: Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Liquid biopsy involves the analysis of biomarkers, such as circulating tumor cells and cell-free DNA, in bodily fluids like blood or urine.

 

  • Liquid biopsy is a minimally invasive diagnostic technique that analyzes biomarkers such as:
    • Circulating Tumor Cells (CTCs)
    • Cell-Free DNA (cfDNA)
    • Exosomes and microRNAs
  • These biomarkers are present in bodily fluids like blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and provide critical information about tumor genetics and progression.
  • Liquid biopsy is particularly useful for early cancer detection, monitoring treatment response, and identifying emerging resistance mutations.
  • It offers a non-invasive alternative to traditional tissue biopsy and allows real-time tracking of cancer dynamics.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Liquid biopsy primarily relies on the analysis of tissue samples obtained through surgical procedures: Incorrect. Traditional biopsy relies on tissue samples obtained surgically, while liquid biopsy analyzes blood or other bodily fluids.

 

Option B. It is mainly used for the diagnosis of infectious diseases and not for cancer detection: Incorrect.Liquid biopsy is predominantly used in cancer detection, monitoring, and targeted therapy selection, rather than infectious disease diagnosis.

 

Option D. Liquid biopsy is only used to determine the exact stage of cancer but not for initial detection: Incorrect.Liquid biopsy is useful for early cancer detection, identifying minimal residual disease (MRD), and tracking tumor progression.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Liquid biopsy is a non-invasive technique that detects tumor biomarkers like CTCs and cfDNA in blood or urine.
  • It is useful for early cancer detection, monitoring treatment response, and identifying resistance mutations.
  • Unlike traditional biopsy, it does not require invasive procedures and can be repeated multiple times.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not classified as a taupathy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Huntington’s disease

 

  • Tauopathies are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the abnormal aggregation of tau protein within neurons, leading to cell dysfunction and death.
  • Tau is a microtubule-associated protein involved in stabilizing neuronal cytoskeleton structures.
  • The major tauopathies include:
    • Alzheimer’s disease – Presence of neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau.
    • Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD-tau) – Tau accumulation in frontotemporal regions, causing progressive dementia.
    • Parkinsonism (including Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration) – Some forms of parkinsonian syndromes show tau pathology.
  • Huntington’s disease (HD), however, is NOT a tauopathy.
    • HD is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats on chromosome 4, leading to toxic accumulation of mutant huntingtin protein, not tau protein.
    • The primary pathology in HD involves striatal degeneration and loss of medium spiny neurons.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Parkinsonism: Parkinson's disease is primarily associated with α-synuclein aggregates in Lewy bodies, but certain atypical parkinsonian syndromes (e.g., Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Corticobasal Degeneration) are tauopathies.

 

Option B. Alzheimer’s disease: Alzheimer’s features neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau, along with β-amyloid plaques.

 

Option C. Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD-tau): FTLD-tau is a major cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and is characterized by tau inclusions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Tauopathies are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by tau protein accumulation.
  • Alzheimer’s disease, FTLD-tau, and some atypical Parkinsonian syndromes (PSP, CBD) are tauopathies.
  • Huntington’s disease is NOT a tauopathy; it is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT) on chromosome 4.

questions.stemHtml: A patient underwent serum electrophoresis whose image is provided. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nephrotic syndrome

 

  • The serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) pattern in the provided image shows low albumin levels and an increased alpha-2 globulin fraction, which is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.
  • Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by:
    • Hypoalbuminemia due to significant protein loss in urine.
    • Increased alpha-2 globulin fraction due to increased hepatic production of α2-macroglobulin and other acute-phase proteins in response to protein loss.
    • Normal or slightly decreased gamma globulin levels (contrast with multiple myeloma).
  • The kidney's inability to retain proteins results in the liver compensating by increasing α2-globulin synthesis, which is a hallmark of nephrotic syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Multiple myeloma: Incorrect.

 

  • In multiple myeloma, the electrophoresis pattern shows a sharp monoclonal spike (M-spike) in the gamma region due to excess immunoglobulin production by malignant plasma cells.
  • This "church spire" peak is absent in the provided image.

 

Option B. Tuberculosis: Incorrect.

 

  • Tuberculosis does not typically cause a characteristic electrophoresis pattern.
  • Chronic inflammatory diseases may show a polyclonal gamma globulin increase, but this pattern is not specific for tuberculosis.

 

Option C. Hepatic cirrhosis: Incorrect.

 

  • In hepatic cirrhosis, albumin is decreased, and there is a polyclonal increase in gamma globulins (β-γ bridging) due to impaired liver function and chronic immune activation.
  • The given electrophoresis pattern lacks this characteristic finding.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by hypoalbuminemia and an increased alpha-2 globulin fraction on serum protein electrophoresis.
  • Multiple myeloma shows an M-spike in the gamma region.
  • Hepatic cirrhosis presents with β-γ bridging due to polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.
  • Serum protein electrophoresis is an essential diagnostic tool in evaluating protein abnormalities in nephrotic syndrome, multiple myeloma, and chronic liver diseases.

questions.stem: In a patient receiving recurrent transfusions for thalassemia, the development of fever and chills is observed during this period, without any evidence of hemolysis. Which of the following measures can help reduce the rate of transfusion reactions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Leuko-reduced RBCs

 

  • This patient is experiencing a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR), a common complication of recurrent transfusions.
  • FNHTR is caused by cytokines released from donor white blood cells (WBCs) that accumulate during blood storage.
  • Leukocyte reduction (Leuko-reduced RBCs) helps by removing most WBCs from the transfused blood, thereby preventing cytokine accumulation and reducing the risk of FNHTR.

 

Key Features of FNHTR:

 

  • Fever and chills during or shortly after transfusion
  • No hemolysis (i.e., no hemoglobinuria, jaundice, or significant drop in hemoglobin)
  • More common in patients requiring multiple transfusions (e.g., thalassemia, sickle cell disease)
  • Prevention: Use of leuko-reduced RBCs

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Irradiation:

 

  • Irradiation of RBCs is done to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD) in immunocompromised patients.
  • It does not prevent febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions.

 

Option B. Antibiotics:

 

  • FNHTR is not an infection, so antibiotics are unnecessary.
  • If the fever persists beyond the transfusion or is associated with hypotension, septic transfusion reaction should be considered instead.

 

Option D. Washed RBCs:

 

  • Washing RBCs removes plasma proteins, which is helpful in IgA-deficient patients at risk of anaphylaxis.
  • It does not prevent FNHTR, which is cytokine-mediated.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) is due to cytokines released from donor WBCs.
  • Leuko-reduced RBC transfusions significantly decrease FNHTR risk.
  • Irradiation prevents TA-GVHD, while washed RBCs are used for IgA-deficient patients with anaphylactic reactions.
  • FNHTR is managed with supportive care (antipyretics) and does not require antibiotics.

 

Prevention –

 

  1. Pre-storage leukoreduction
  2. NSAIDs, if persistent fever 
  3. Use of platelet additive solution
  4. Plasma reduced or washed products if severe reactions
  5. Restrictive transfusion approach in high-risk patients

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with cancer. The research revealed the role played by a tumor suppressor gene SMAD4. Which of the following is the predominant role played by this gene in the tumor cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Inhibition of mitogenic pathway

 

  • SMAD4 is a tumor suppressor gene that plays a crucial role in the TGF-β (Transforming Growth Factor-beta) signaling pathway.
  • It regulates cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis, particularly by inhibiting the mitogenic (growth-promoting) pathways.
  • Loss of SMAD4 function leads to uncontrolled cellular proliferation, contributing to tumorigenesis.
  • Common cancers associated with SMAD4 mutations include:
    • Juvenile polyposis syndrome (hereditary disorder)
    • Pancreatic cancer
    • Colorectal cancer

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. DNA Repair 

 

  • SMAD4 does not play a direct role in DNA repair.
  • DNA repair genes include BRCA1, BRCA2, MLH1, and MSH2 (linked to microsatellite instability).

 

Option B. Inhibition of Angiogenesis 

 

  • Angiogenesis inhibitors (like VHL tumor suppressor gene) prevent tumor blood supply formation.
  • SMAD4 does not have a direct role in angiogenesis inhibition.

 

Option C. Inhibition of Invasion 

 

  • Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) contributes to tumor invasion, not SMAD4.
  • SMAD4 primarily regulates growth signaling, not invasion directly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • SMAD4 is a tumor suppressor gene involved in the TGF-β signaling pathway.
  • Its primary role is to inhibit mitogenic (growth-promoting) pathways.
  • Mutations in SMAD4 are linked to juvenile polyposis syndrome, pancreatic cancer, and colorectal cancer.
  • It is not directly involved in DNA repair, angiogenesis inhibition, or tumor invasion.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male Kabir presents with complaints of yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclerae for the past few days. He denies any recent fever, abdominal pain, or dark urine. On examination, there is jaundice noted. Laboratory tests reveal elevated levels of unconjugated bilirubin in the serum with normal hemoglobin. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Gilbert's syndrome

 

  • The key findings in this patient include isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal hemoglobin levels and no signs of hemolysis or liver dysfunction.
  • Gilbert's syndrome is a benign inherited disorder caused by reduced activity of the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), which leads to impaired bilirubin conjugation in the liver.
  • Typical triggers for jaundice in Gilbert's syndrome include:
    • Fasting or stress
    • Infections
    • Exertion or dehydration
    • Menstruation
  • Patients are otherwise healthy, and the condition is diagnosed incidentally.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemolytic Anemia 

 

  • Hemolysis leads to increased RBC breakdown, resulting in unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
  • However, this patient has normal hemoglobin, ruling out hemolysis.

 

Option B. Alcoholic Liver Disease 

 

  • Alcoholic liver disease causes both conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to liver dysfunction.
  • This patient has isolated unconjugated bilirubin elevation, and no history of alcohol use is given.

 

Option C. Biliary Obstruction 

 

  • Biliary obstruction leads to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not unconjugated.
  • It is usually associated with pale stools, dark urine, and itching, which are absent in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Gilbert’s syndrome is a common, benign cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced UGT1A1 enzyme activity.
  • It is often triggered by stress, fasting, infections, or exertion and presents without liver dysfunction or hemolysis.
  • It does not require treatment and is managed with reassurance.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a four-week history of productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and low-grade fever. Physical examination reveals diminished breath sounds over the right lower lung field. A chest X-ray shows a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lung abscess

 

  • The cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level on chest X-ray is characteristic of lung abscess.
  • Lung abscesses are localized areas of necrotizing infection in the lung parenchyma, often due to aspiration of oropharyngeal contents.
  • The most common predisposing factors include:
    • Aspiration (most common cause)
    • Alcoholism (due to impaired cough reflex)
    • Neurological disorders (stroke, seizures)
    • Poor dental hygiene (leading to anaerobic bacterial colonization)
  • The right bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, making the right lower lobe the most common site for aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Tuberculosis 

 

  • Tuberculosis can cause cavitary lesions, but it usually affects the upper lobes.
  • TB cavities lack an air-fluid level unless there is a secondary infection.

 

Option B. Lung Cancer 

 

  • Lung cancer can mimic cavitary lesions, but malignancies are typically associated with weight loss, hemoptysis, and a mass effect rather than an air-fluid level.

 

Option C. Pulmonary Embolism 

 

  • PE can lead to infarction and cavitation, but air-fluid levels are uncommon.
  • Patients with PE often present with sudden onset dyspnea, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain, which is not the primary presentation here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Lung abscess is characterized by a cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level on imaging, commonly in the right lower lobe due to aspiration.
  • Aspiration pneumonia is the most common cause, particularly in patients with altered consciousness (alcoholism, stroke, seizures, anesthesia).

questions.stem: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) HbA2 levels

 

This patient has microcytic hypochromic anemia, which can be caused by:

 

  1. Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA)
  2. Thalassemia (usually β-thalassemia minor)
  3. Anemia of Chronic Disease (AOCD)
  4. Sideroblastic Anemia

 

To differentiate between these conditions, we use:

 

  • MCV (low in all microcytic anemias)
  • RBC count (normal/increased in thalassemia, decreased in IDA/AOCD)
  • Mentzer Index → MCV/RBC count
    • < 13 → Thalassemia (Minor)
    • > 13 → Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA)
    • In this case: 60 ÷ 5.2 = ~11.5 → Suggestive of thalassemia
  • β-thalassemia minor is confirmed by increased HbA2 (>3.5%) on hemoglobin electrophoresis.
  • This is critical because iron supplementation does not help thalassemia, but it is necessary in IDA.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serum Ferritin Levels:

 

  • Ferritin is low in IDA, but normal in thalassemia minor.
  • Since the Mentzer Index suggests thalassemia, ferritin is not the best next step.

 

Option C. Serum Folate Levels: 

 

  • Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia (MCV > 100 fL), not microcytic anemia.

 

Option D. Serum Homocysteine Levels: 

 

  • Homocysteine levels are elevated in B12 or folate deficiency, but this patient has microcytic anemia, ruling out both.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Mentzer Index (<13 suggests thalassemia, >13 suggests IDA).
  • HbA2 levels are crucial in diagnosing β-thalassemia minor.
  • Iron deficiency anemia responds to iron therapy, whereas thalassemia does not.

questions.stem: A patient with occupational exposure to benzene presents with repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature. This occupational exposure will predispose him to which of the following cancers?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia 

 

Benzene Exposure and Hematologic Malignancies

 

  • Benzene is a known carcinogen that affects bone marrow, leading to:
    • Leukemia (especially acute leukemias like ALL and AML)
    • Aplastic anemia
    • Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)
  • Mechanism:
    • Benzene interferes with hematopoiesis → leading to bone marrow failure → pancytopenia
    • Causes DNA damage leading to chromosomal abnormalities → promotes leukemic transformation
  • Symptoms in this patient (infection, weight loss, fever, fatigue) suggest bone marrow suppression and hematologic malignancy (leukemia).
  • Benzene exposure is strongly linked to acute leukemias, particularly Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).
  • Patients with benzene exposure often develop acute leukemias rather than chronic leukemias.
  • The presence of infections, anemia, and weight loss suggests leukemia rather than solid tumors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bladder Cancer 

 

  • Bladder cancer is associated with exposure to benzidine and aniline dyes (not benzene).
  • Seen in rubber, dye, and textile industry workers.
  • Strongly linked to aromatic amines, smoking, and Schistosoma infection.

 

Option B. Lung Cancer 

 

  • Lung cancer is mainly linked to smoking, asbestos, and radon gas exposure.
  • Benzene is not a significant risk factor for lung cancer.

 

Option D. Basal Cell Cancer 

 

  • Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is caused by UV radiation and is common in fair-skinned individuals with sun exposure.
  • Heavy metal exposure (e.g., arsenic) is also associated with BCC.
  • Benzene is not a known cause of basal cell carcinoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Benzene exposure increases the risk of acute leukemias (ALL and AML).
  • Benzidine and aniline dyes cause bladder cancer.
  • Lung cancer is primarily linked to smoking, asbestos, and radon exposure.
  • Basal cell carcinoma is caused by UV radiation and heavy metals (e.g., arsenic).

questions.stem: A girl presents with short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swelling of the ankle, and increased carrying angle. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Turner syndrome

 

Turner syndrome is a genetic disorder characterized by the partial or complete absence of one X chromosome (45, X karyotype). It presents with distinctive physical features, including:

 

  • Short stature – One of the most common findings in Turner syndrome.
  • Webbed neck – Due to congenital lymphedema, leading to redundant skin folds.
  • Shield-shaped chest – Broad chest with widely spaced nipples.
  • Swelling of the ankles – Due to lymphedema, often seen at birth.
  • Increased carrying angle (Cubitus valgus) – A widened angle between the arm and forearm.
  • Thick calves – Often part of the generalized lymphedema seen in these patients.

 

In addition to these physical features, Turner syndrome is associated with streak gonads, meaning the gonadal tissue is replaced by fibrous tissue, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Down syndrome: Incorrect. Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) presents with characteristic features such as flat facial profile, upward slanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, hypotonia, and intellectual disability. While short stature can be seen, features like a webbed neck and streak gonads are not characteristic of Down syndrome.

 

Option C. Patau syndrome: Incorrect. Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) presents with severe midline defects, including holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, and congenital heart defects. The features described in the question are not consistent with Patau syndrome.

 

Option D. Edward syndrome: Incorrect. Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18) is characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and congenital heart defects. The findings described in the question do not align with this condition.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Turner syndrome should be suspected in a female with short stature, webbed neck, shield-shaped chest, lymphedema, and increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus). A key additional finding is streak gonads, leading to primary ovarian failure and infertility.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass. Which of the following can be the likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Thymoma

 

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare hematologic disorder characterized by selective depletion of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, leading to severe anemia with normal white blood cells and platelets. PRCA is often associated with thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland.

 

  • Key association: PRCA has a well-established link with thymoma, as thymomas can produce autoantibodies or T-cell mediated immune dysfunction that suppresses erythropoiesis.
  • Mediastinal mass: The presence of a mediastinal mass in an elderly patient with PRCA strongly suggests a thymoma.
  • Thymomas and paraneoplastic syndromes: Thymomas are also linked to myasthenia gravis, hypogammaglobulinemia, and other autoimmune disorders.

 

Thus, in a patient presenting with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass, thymoma is the most likely underlying cause.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Germ cell tumor: Germ cell tumors, especially extragonadal germ cell tumors, can present as mediastinal masses. However, they are more commonly associated with elevated tumor markers (AFP, β-hCG) and do not typically cause pure red cell aplasia.

 

Option B. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present with mediastinal involvement but is not strongly associated with pure red cell aplasia. Instead, it may cause systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss (B symptoms).

 

Option C. Bronchogenic carcinoma: Bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer) can present as a mediastinal mass, but it is typically associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like hypercalcemia (PTHrP secretion) or SIADH, rather than PRCA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is strongly associated with thymoma. If a patient presents with PRCA and a mediastinal mass, thymoma should be the first consideration.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male presents with fever, fatigue, and night sweats. He has a history of mitral valve prolapse. On auscultation, a holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. His echocardiography revealed large, friable and irregular vegetations on heart valves. What is the likely diagnosis of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Infective endocarditis 

 

The patient presents with fever, fatigue, and night sweats, which are constitutional symptoms of an infectious process. Additionally, he has a history of mitral valve prolapse, which is a known risk factor for infective endocarditis (IE).

 

Key findings that support infective endocarditis include:

 

  • Holosystolic murmur at the apex – Suggests mitral regurgitation, commonly seen in IE.
  • Large, friable, and irregular vegetations on echocardiography – This is characteristic of infective endocarditis, particularly with high embolic potential.
  • Mitral valve involvement – The mitral valve is the most commonly affected valve in native valve endocarditis, especially in individuals with underlying mitral valve prolapse.

 

Additionally, septic embolism (embolic infarcts in different organs) is a potential complication due to friable vegetations, further supporting the diagnosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Rheumatic heart disease: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is caused by immune-mediated damage following streptococcal infection and leads to small, firm vegetations along the line of closure of the valves. This patient’s echocardiographic findings (large, friable, irregular vegetations) are not consistent with RHD.

 

Option C. Libman-Sacks endocarditis: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and causes sterile, verrucous vegetations on both sides of the valve leaflets. The patient has no signs of SLE, making this an unlikely diagnosis.

 

Option D. Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE): NBTE (also called marantic endocarditis) is associated with malignancies and hypercoagulable states, forming sterile, platelet-rich thrombi without significant inflammation. This patient has infectious features (fever, fatigue, night sweats), making NBTE unlikely.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Infective endocarditis should be suspected in patients with fever, a new murmur, and echocardiographic evidence of large, friable vegetations. Mitral valve prolapse is a known predisposing factor for IE.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child was brought to the hospital with complaints of fever, rash and swelling of her hands and feet since past 5 days. There is desquamative skin rash, edema of hands and feet, erythema of palms and soles, oral erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the likely condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Kawasaki disease

 

Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute vasculitis of unknown etiology that primarily affects children under 5 years of age. It is diagnosed based on clinical criteria, which include fever for at least 5 days along with at least four of the following five features:

 

  1. Polymorphous rash – Desquamative rash, often beginning in the perineal region.
  2. Edema and erythema of hands and feet – Swelling and redness, followed by peeling in later stages.
  3. Oral mucosal involvement – Red, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, and pharyngeal erythema.
  4. Bilateral, non-purulent conjunctivitis – Eye redness without discharge.
  5. Cervical lymphadenopathy – At least one enlarged lymph node >1.5 cm.

 

This child's presentation aligns perfectly with Kawasaki disease. The most dangerous complication of KD is coronary artery aneurysm, which can lead to myocardial infarction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Measles: 

 

  • Measles presents with high fever, Koplik spots, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a maculopapular rash that spreads cephalocaudally (from face downward). It does not cause hand/foot edema or desquamation.

 

Option C. Scarlet fever: Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS) and is associated with:

 

  • Sandpaper-like rash
  • Strawberry tongue
  • Pastia’s lines (linear rash in skin folds)
  • Pharyngitis
    Unlike Kawasaki disease, it does not cause conjunctivitis, desquamation, or limb edema.

 

Option D. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP): HSP is an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis that presents with:

 

  • Palpable purpura (non-blanching rash, often on buttocks and legs)
  • Arthritis/arthralgia
  • Abdominal pain and renal involvement (IgA nephropathy)
    Unlike Kawasaki disease, HSP does not involve conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, or cervical lymphadenopathy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Kawasaki disease should be suspected in any child with prolonged fever (≥5 days), rash, limb edema, conjunctivitis, oral erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. The most dangerous complication is coronary artery aneurysm leading to myocardial infarction, and treatment includes IVIG and aspirin.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. Duodenal biopsy of the patient showed crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. This patient is kept under regular follow-up to diagnose which of the following malignancies?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Enteric T cell lymphoma 

 

The patient’s clinical history and biopsy findings are highly suggestive of celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy).

 

  • Key histological features of celiac disease include:
    • Villous atrophy – Loss of normal intestinal architecture.
    • Crypt hyperplasia – Increased depth of intestinal crypts.
    • Infiltration of CD8+ T cells in the lamina propria.
  • Serologic markers of celiac disease include:
    • Anti-endomysial antibodies
    • Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies

 

Celiac disease is associated with an increased risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), a rare but aggressive malignancy. Patients who continue to consume gluten despite being diagnosed with celiac disease are at a particularly high risk.

 

Thus, regular follow-up is necessary to monitor for EATL development in patients with refractory or long-standing celiac disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. MALToma: MALT (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue) lymphoma is associated with H. pylori infection and primarily affects the stomach, not the small intestine. It is not linked to celiac disease.

 

Option B. Gastric adenocarcinoma: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection, chronic atrophic gastritis, and certain genetic factors. It is not the primary malignancy of concern in celiac disease patients.

 

Option C. Adenocarcinoma of the colon: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is primarily associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Lynch syndrome, and chronic inflammatory conditions like ulcerative colitis. It is not the main malignancy associated with celiac disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Patients with celiac disease, particularly those with persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet, are at an increased risk for enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), a serious and aggressive malignancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Huntington's chorea?

options.label: A
options.text: There is loss of function type of mutation

options.label: B
options.text: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder

options.label: C
options.text: There are abnormal repeats of CUG

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 6

questions.answerText: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder

 

Huntington's chorea is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG on chromosome 4 in the HTT gene. The CAG repeats lead to the production of a toxic protein called huntingtin, which causes progressive neuronal degeneration, particularly in the caudate nucleus and putamen of the brain.

 

Key features of the disorder:

 

  • Trinucleotide repeat disorder: Huntington's chorea involves an increase in CAG repeats, which leads to a gain-of-function mutation.
  • Anticipation: The severity of the disease increases, and onset occurs earlier in successive generations due to further expansion of the trinucleotide repeats.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. There is loss of function type of mutation: This is incorrect. Huntington's disease involves a gain-of-function mutation, as the abnormal protein (huntingtin) disrupts normal cellular processes.

 

Option C. There are abnormal repeats of CUG: This is incorrect. The trinucleotide repeats in Huntington's disease are CAG, not CUG. CUG repeats are associated with conditions like myotonic dystrophy.

 

Option D. Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 6: This is incorrect. The mutation occurs on chromosome 4, not chromosome 6.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide repeat disorder involving CAG repeats on chromosome 4. It leads to a gain-of-function mutation, causing a toxic protein that results in neurodegeneration and anticipation across generations.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with a painless abdominal mass, abdominal pain, and hematuria. On physical examination, a large, palpable, non-tender abdominal mass is noted. Which of the following is not correct about this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Nephrogenic rests are a precursor lesion

options.label: B
options.text: Gene affected in this condition is present on short arm of chr11

options.label: C
options.text: Wild type of P53 is associated with poor prognosis

options.label: D
options.text: Histology reveals blastemal, stromal & epithelial components

questions.answerText: Wild type of P53 is associated with poor prognosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Wild type of P53 is associated with poor prognosis

 

  • P53 is a tumor suppressor gene, and its mutation (not the wild type) is associated with poor prognosis in Wilms tumor.
  • Anaplasia in Wilms tumor is linked to P53 mutation, leading to worse outcomes.
  • Wild-type (normal) P53 is not associated with poor prognosis; instead, it helps in tumor suppression. 
  • p53 mutation is seen in the more aggressive anaplastic subtype.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nephrogenic rests are a precursor lesion: Correct. Nephrogenic rests are clusters of embryonic kidney cells that fail to differentiate properly and serve as precursor lesions for Wilms tumor.

 

 Option B. Gene affected in this condition is present on short arm of chromosome 11: Correct. Wilms tumor is associated with WT1 and WT2 gene mutations, both located on chromosome 11p.

 

Option D. Histology reveals blastemal, stromal & epithelial components: Correct. Wilms tumor has a characteristic triphasic histology, consisting of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial components.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wilms tumor is a common childhood renal malignancy associated with mutations in WT1 and WT2 on chromosome 11p. It has a triphasic histology and can arise from nephrogenic rests. Poor prognosis is associated with P53 mutation and anaplasia, not the wild-type (normal) P53.
